query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing interstitial oxygen into the Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy will disrupt long‐range atomic order via formation of ordered oxygen complexes and, as a consequence, improve its glass-forming ability compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy prepared by arc-melting and conventional casting
generation.intervention: Interstitial oxygen doping (as performed by adding TiO2 during alloy synthesis to form an oxygen-doped (O-2 HEA) variant)
generation.conditions: Processing by repeated arc-melting and drop-casting into a water-cooled copper mold, under conditions similar to those used for interstitial doping in the referenced study; rapid quenching rates to promote amorphization
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered oxygen complexes that introduce local lattice distortions and disruptions in long-range atomic order
generation.mechanism: The ordered oxygen complexes are hypothesized to act as local ‘defects’ that inhibit the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during cooling, thereby enhancing the alloy’s ability to form a glassy (amorphous) structure
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped base HEA, the oxygen-doped HEA will exhibit an increased glass-forming range or a lower crystallization onset temperature during cooling, indicating enhanced glass-forming ability
generation.baseline: Undoped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA synthesized under identical conditions
generation.boundary: The effect is expected within a limited range of oxygen doping (roughly at levels similar to those used to achieve ordered oxygen complexes in the damping study), and the influence of oxygen on crystallization kinetics must be evaluated under comparable rapid-quenching processing conditions
generation.uncertainty: The supporting evidence focuses on damping and mechanical properties rather than glass formation. While interstitial doping is known in some metallic systems to disrupt crystallization, it remains uncertain whether the ordered oxygen complexes in this HEA will extend to a meaningful enhancement in glass-forming ability. Further experimental verification is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloys via arc-melting: one undoped and the other doped with oxygen (using TiO2 with concentrations similar to the O-2 HEA synthesis). Rapidly quench both sets via drop-casting into a water-cooled mold. Characterize the resulting samples using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to evaluate the presence of amorphous versus crystalline phases and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the onset temperature of crystallization.
measurements: XRD patterns to assess amorphous (broad halo) vs crystalline (sharp peaks) structure
DSC scans to measure the glass transition and crystallization exotherms (onset and peak temperatures)
Microstructural analysis via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) if necessary
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant extension of the glass-forming range (e.g., lower crystallization onset temperature or increased amorphous fraction) relative to the undoped base alloy, then the hypothesis that interstitial oxygen improves glass-forming ability in this HEA will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
